headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Female Genital Mutilation (FGM)
headings.content: Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) encompasses all procedures involving partial or total removal of the external female genitalia or other injury to the female genital organs for non-medical reasons. As nursing students in Nigeria, understanding this definition is vital because FGM is recognized globally and nationally as a violation of the human rights of girls and women. It is deeply rooted in gender inequality and power imbalances, often performed under the guise of cultural preservation, rite of passage, or ensuring chastity and hygiene. The World Health Organization classifies FGM into distinct types, all of which cause severe physical and psychological trauma with no documented health benefits. In the Nigerian context, nurses frequently encounter clients who have undergone FGM or are at risk within specific ethnic groups and geographic regions. Recognizing that the practice is driven by socio-cultural norms rather than medical necessity allows healthcare professionals to approach the issue with both clinical precision and cultural sensitivity. Nurses must understand that FGM is not just a localized problem of bleeding or infection, but a systemic public health concern that perpetuates gender-based violence. By grasping the foundational definition, nursing students prepare themselves to advocate effectively, educate families, and provide comprehensive, non-judgmental care to affected populations across Nigerian healthcare settings, from primary health care clinics to tertiary teaching hospitals.

headings.title: Types and Classifications of FGM
headings.content: The World Health Organization classifies Female Genital Mutilation into four major types, a critical knowledge base for Nigerian nursing students assessing trauma in female patients. Type I, often referred to as clitoridectomy, involves the partial or total removal of the clitoris and/or the prepuce. Type II, or excision, entails the partial or total removal of the clitoris and the labia minora, with or without excision of the labia majora. Type III, the most severe form known as infibulation, involves narrowing of the vaginal orifice through the creation of a covering seal. This seal is formed by cutting and repositioning the labia minora or labia majora, sometimes through stitching, with or without removal of the clitoris. Type IV encompasses all other harmful procedures to the female genitalia for non-medical purposes, such as pricking, piercing, incising, scraping, and cauterization. Understanding these classifications helps nurses accurately document physical examination findings, anticipate specific clinical complications, and plan individualized nursing care. For example, a patient with Type III infibulation will require specialized care during menstruation, coitus, and particularly during obstetric labor, where defibulation may be necessary. Recognizing the specific type of FGM performed aids healthcare professionals in tailoring psychological counseling, surgical interventions, and preventative education for vulnerable young girls presenting to clinics.

headings.title: Cultural Drivers and Societal Perceptions in Nigeria
headings.content: Cultural drivers and societal perceptions play a massive role in the perpetuation of Female Genital Mutilation across various communities in Nigeria. For nursing students, understanding these underlying beliefs is essential for effective communication and behavior change communication. Many communities practice FGM because it is deeply embedded in tradition, viewed as a necessary rite of passage into womanhood, and associated with cultural identity. Societal perceptions frequently link the practice to female purity, modesty, chastity, and fidelity, with the false belief that an uncircumcised female is promiscuous or unclean. Furthermore, socio-cultural pressures enforce compliance; families fear social exclusion, stigmatization, or the inability of their daughters to secure marriage if they refuse to conform. In some regions, economic security through marriage depends on adherence to these traditional norms. Additionally, misconceptions regarding religion, hygiene, and enhanced male sexual pleasure continue to fuel the practice despite lack of theological or scientific backing. Nurses must recognize that confronting FGM requires more than condemnation; it demands empathetic engagement with community leaders, elders, and traditional birth attendants who hold sway over these beliefs. By addressing the root cultural drivers respectfully yet firmly, healthcare professionals can champion community-led abandonment initiatives and protect young girls from undergoing this harmful traditional practice.

headings.title: Immediate and Long-Term Health Complications
headings.content: Female Genital Mutilation inflicts a wide spectrum of immediate and long-term health complications that demand expert nursing management. Immediate complications often arise from the use of crude, unsterilized instruments such as razor blades, knives, or broken glass by traditional practitioners without anesthesia. These include severe acute pain, excessive hemorrhage that can lead to hypovolemic shock, shock from neurogenic pain, acute urinary retention due to swelling or pain, local and systemic infections like tetanus and sepsis, and injury to adjacent pelvic organs such as the urethra, vagina, and rectum. Long-term complications manifest over years and profoundly affect female reproductive and urinary health. Chronic pain, recurrent urinary tract infections, dysuria, formation of dermoid cysts, keloid scar formation, and dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse) are frequently reported. In obstetric settings, survivors face prolonged labor, perineal tears, obstetric fistula, postpartum hemorrhage, and increased risk of perinatal asphyxia or neonatal death. Nigerian nurses must be clinically adept at identifying these complications during routine assessments, managing acute hemorrhage, providing pain relief, and offering specialized gynecological care. Recognizing these extensive physical sequelae underscores the critical importance of primary prevention and holistic, multidisciplinary support for survivors presenting in clinical practice.

headings.title: Psychological and Psychosexual Impact on Women and Girls
headings.content: Beyond the physical morbidity, Female Genital Mutilation leaves profound psychological and psychosexual scars on women and girls. Nursing students must appreciate the mental health dimensions of FGM, as psychological trauma is often lifelong and debilitating. Survivors frequently experience post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), severe anxiety, chronic depression, panic attacks, and low self-esteem stemming from the betrayal of trust, violation of bodily integrity, and the sheer terror associated with the procedure during childhood or adolescence. Psychosexually, the removal of or damage to highly sensitive genital tissue, particularly the clitoris, results in chronic dyspareunia, anorgasmia (inability to achieve orgasm), diminished sexual desire, and overall sexual dysfunction. This can severely strain marital relationships and contribute to marital discord, psychological distress, and social isolation. Nurses must adopt a trauma-informed care approach when interacting with survivors, creating a safe, confidential, and empathetic environment that encourages emotional expression. Mental health screening, supportive counseling, and psychological referrals should be integrated into routine nursing care for affected women. Understanding these deeply personal impacts enables Nigerian nurses to provide holistic care that addresses both the physical wounds and the invisible emotional trauma carried by survivors.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Identification of Survivors
headings.content: Nursing assessment and the identification of FGM survivors require high levels of clinical observation, cultural competence, and sensitive communication skills. Nigerian nurses encounter women during antenatal visits, labor and delivery, gynecological examinations, and pediatric assessments where signs of FGM may be incidentally discovered or suspected. When conducting history-taking and physical examinations, nurses must maintain absolute confidentiality, privacy, and a non-judgmental attitude to build trust with the patient. Assessment involves observing for scar tissue, asymmetry, missing anatomical structures of the external genitalia, or signs of infibulation such as a narrowed vaginal opening. Nurses should be vigilant for clinical red flags, including chronic pelvic pain, recurrent urinary tract infections, difficulties during menstrual flow, and expressions of psychological distress or fear during pelvic exams. It is vital to use clear, gentle language when asking about genital cutting, avoiding stigmatizing terminology. For pediatric nurses, assessing young girls during routine immunization or well-child visits for signs of impending risk—such as upcoming cultural ceremonies or family travel plans to rural areas during holiday periods—allows for proactive intervention and child protection. Effective nursing assessment bridges the gap between clinical presentation and holistic advocacy, ensuring that hidden trauma is brought to light and appropriately managed.

headings.title: Community Health Nursing Interventions and Advocacy
headings.content: Community health nursing interventions and advocacy are powerful tools in the global and national effort to eradicate Female Genital Mutilation. Community health nurses in Nigeria are uniquely positioned to spearhead grassroots educational campaigns, health talks, and outreach programs that debunk myths surrounding FGM. These interventions focus on educating mothers, community leaders, youth groups, and religious figures about the severe health complications and legal consequences of the practice. Nurses work collaboratively with local stakeholders to design culturally acceptable alternatives, such as alternative rites of passage that celebrate a young girl's transition into adulthood without bodily harm or genital cutting. Advocacy also involves empowering women economically and educationally, recognizing that gender empowerment directly reduces the reliance on harmful traditional practices. Furthermore, community health nurses establish support groups for survivors, providing a safe space for healing, peer counseling, and referral to psychological and medical services. By engaging communities in dialogue rather than confrontation, nurses foster sustainable behavior change and build local champions who advocate against FGM from within their own cultural frameworks, ensuring long-term protection for future generations of Nigerian girls.

headings.title: Legal Frameworks and Policies Against FGM in Nigeria
headings.content: Legal frameworks and policies against Female Genital Mutilation in Nigeria provide the formal backing necessary to protect women and girls from violence and abuse. Nursing students must be well-informed about these legal instruments to understand their professional obligations in reporting and patient advocacy. At the national level, the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act, signed into law in 2015, explicitly prohibits FGM, prescribing penalties of imprisonment and fines for perpetrators and anyone who incites, aids, or abets the practice. Additionally, several states across Nigeria have enacted state-specific child rights laws and anti-FGM legislations that criminalize the procedure. From a professional standpoint, the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN) and medical ethics codes strictly prohibit nurses and midwives from performing FGM in any healthcare setting, a malpractice known as medicalization of FGM. Nurses must recognize that performing or abetting FGM is a gross professional misconduct that leads to license revocation and legal prosecution. Understanding these legal structures empowers nurses to act as child protection advocates, cooperate with legal authorities when abuse is identified, and educate families on the legal penalties associated with violating anti-FGM laws across the country.
